title: Risk Stratification for Early Detection of Diabetes and Hypertension in Resource-Limited Settings: Machine Learning Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: The impending scale up of noncommunicable disease screening programs in low- and middle-income countries coupled with limited health resources require that such programs be as accurate as possible at identifying patients at high risk. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to develop machine learning-based risk stratification algorithms for diabetes and hypertension that are tailored for the at-risk population served by community-based screening programs in low-resource settings. METHODS: We trained and tested our models by using data from 2278 patients collected by community health workers through door-to-door and camp-based screenings in the urban slums of Hyderabad, India between July 14, 2015 and April 21, 2018. We determined the best models for predicting short-term (2-month) risk of diabetes and hypertension (a model for diabetes and a model for hypertension) and compared these models to previously developed risk scores from the United States and the United Kingdom by using prediction accuracy as characterized by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and the number of false negatives. RESULTS: We found that models based on random forest had the highest prediction accuracy for both diseases and were able to outperform the US and UK risk scores in terms of AUC by 35.5% for diabetes (improvement of 0.239 from 0.671 to 0.910) and 13.5% for hypertension (improvement of 0.094 from 0.698 to 0.792). For a fixed screening specificity of 0.9, the random forest model was able to reduce the expected number of false negatives by 620 patients per 1000 screenings for diabetes and 220 patients per 1000 screenings for hypertension. This improvement reduces the cost of incorrect risk stratification by US $1.99 (or 35%) per screening for diabetes and US $1.60 (or 21%) per screening for hypertension. CONCLUSIONS: In the next decade, health systems in many countries are planning to spend significant resources on noncommunicable disease screening programs and our study demonstrates that machine learning models can be leveraged by these programs to effectively utilize limited resources by improving risk stratification.

summary.oneLiner: Machine learning models significantly improve diabetes and hypertension risk stratification in low-resource settings compared to traditional risk scores from high-income countries.
summary.overview: Community-based health screening in low-income regions often uses risk assessment models developed for high-income countries, which struggle to account for local lifestyle and socioeconomic differences. This study developed custom machine learning algorithms for identifying diabetes and hypertension in urban Indian slums using simple, field-collected data. The researchers found that their 'random forest' models—a type of computer algorithm that uses many decision trees to make predictions—performed significantly better than existing models from the US and UK. By providing more accurate risk scores, these models can help health systems better allocate limited resources and reduce the high costs associated with missing diagnoses.
summary.question: Can machine learning-based risk stratification models, specifically tailored for community-based screening programs in low-resource settings, improve the identification of diabetes and hypertension compared to traditional risk scores?
summary.method: The researchers trained and tested five machine learning models (decision trees, regularized logistic regression, K-nearest neighbors, random forest, and AdaBoost) and compared their performance against baseline risk scores from the US and UK using 10-fold cross-validation and receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC).
summary.data: Retrospective data from 2,278 patients collected by community health workers in urban slums in Hyderabad, India, between July 2015 and April 2018.
findings: Random forest models achieved the highest prediction accuracy for both diseases, outperforming the best baseline approaches by 35.5% for diabetes and 13.5% for hypertension.
The random forest model significantly reduced the expected number of false negatives per 1,000 screenings, by 620 for diabetes and 220 for hypertension, at a fixed specificity of 0.9.
The models reduced the expected cost of incorrect risk stratification by 35% for diabetes and 21% for hypertension.
A random forest model using only simple questionnaire-based features could capture 87% of the accuracy achieved by a model using all available clinical measurements.
Traditional risk scores from the US and UK performed poorly in the Indian setting, even after being retrained with local data.
summary.whyItMatters: The findings suggest that health systems in developing nations can improve the effectiveness of their screening programs—and save significant costs—by deploying local, data-driven machine learning models on mobile devices, rather than relying on imported risk assessment tools.
